ClassHub: Collaborative Study Platform for University Students
A real-time collaborative platform where every feature (chat, Q&A, file sharing, and study session scheduling) is scoped per class, built with React and Firebase.

University students juggle class-specific discussions, course material, and study coordination across disconnected tools (group chats, email threads, shared drives) with no single space scoped to *this class, this semester.* **ClassHub** is a real-time platform where every feature (chat, Q&A, file sharing, and study session scheduling) is scoped per class. Students browse and join classes via a live course-catalog integration, then collaborate inside class-specific feeds that update instantly for everyone enrolled.
Live Demo View on GitHub View Presentation
### Architecture
Data Model
Firestore is structured as classes/{"{classId}"}/{"{chat|qa|sessions|resources}"}/..., with nested replies and messages subcollections. Every piece of content is namespaced to its class rather than living in flat global collections, so isolating one class's feed from another is structural, not filtered client-side.
Real-time Sync
All major views (chat, Q&A, session lists, in-session chat) subscribe via Firestore onSnapshot listeners rather than polling, so messages, votes, and replies appear instantly for every connected client. Firestore is configured with persistentLocalCache + multi-tab manager for offline support and fast reloads in production, with a long-polling fallback in local dev to work around a WebChannel/React 19 StrictMode double-invocation issue.
Security Rules
Firestore and Storage rules enforce access control server-side: authenticated reads, ownership checks on writes/deletes (authorId == request.auth.uid), and a default-deny fallback rule, with a 20 MB upload cap on Storage.
Auth
Passwordless email-link sign-in restricted to university email addresses, avoiding password management entirely.
External Data Integration
Course catalog data is pulled from a third-party academic data API (Paper.nu) through a Cloud Functions proxy (to dodge CORS and add caching headers), normalized client-side, and cached in localStorage with a schema-version key so stale shapes self-invalidate on the next fetch.
Local Dev Workflow
Full Firebase Emulator Suite (Firestore, Auth, Storage) wired into the app via hostname detection, so the team could develop and test against realistic backend behavior without touching production data.
### Design System **Token system:** Built a custom design token system in Tailwind config rather than using default colors: a defined brand purple scale (`brand`, `brand-hover`, `brand-light`), semantic text/background/border tokens (`primary`, `sub`, `muted`, `line`, `subtle`), and purpose-specific border radii (`badge`, `btn`, `card`, `modal`, `avatar`) so spacing and rounding stayed consistent across cards, modals, and chips. **Component patterns:** Reusable Tag/Avatar/badge primitives with a fixed semantic color palette (purple/teal/green/orange/pink/blue) deterministically assigned per user, so the same person's avatar color stays consistent across chat, Q&A, and session rosters. **Layout:** Persistent sidebar (class list, navigation) + header + main content + contextual right sidebar, with modal-based flows (course discovery, create-session) layered on top via React Router's background-location pattern. ### My Role As **Project Manager**, I led a team of student engineers through the full build, from defining the product scope and feature set to setting the technical architecture and reviewing the team's work into production. I also worked hands-on in the codebase, building out the core Firebase layer: the per-class Firestore data model, passwordless email-link authentication, real-time chat/Q&A/study-session features, security rules for access control, and the deployment pipeline (Emulator Suite for local dev, Hosting + Cloud Functions for production). A searchable, structured database for Northwestern course and professor evaluations, turning locked PDF reports into something students can actually use.

After every class, Northwestern students fill out CTECs (Course and Teacher Evaluations): 1–6 scale ratings, structured feedback, and written comments. That data is real and detailed, but it's locked inside long, unsearchable PDF reports. There's no way to compare professors, filter by department, or ask a quick question like "is the workload heavy?" without reading the whole document. **CTEC Searcher** turns that PDF archive into something closer to "RateMyProfessor, but structured and data-driven." Students search and filter course offerings by department, level, and term, sort by any of five rating dimensions (instruction quality, course rating, amount learned, intellectual challenge, prior interest), and drill into a course page showing rating distributions, time-survey data, demographics, and raw student comments, plus an AI assistant that answers questions grounded only in that course's actual reviews.
Rapidly search for courses, professors, or departments
Easy to read and navigate UI that quickly and clearly communicates relevant information
Use AI to summarize comments instead of reading through one by one
### Architecture
Data Model
A relational schema (Professor, Course, CourseOffering, Question, QuestionDistribution, Comment) served through Firebase Data Connect over Cloud SQL Postgres. GraphQL-defined types generate fully typed query/mutation clients consumed directly by React hooks, so the schema is the single source of truth from database to UI.
Search, Filter, Sort
Client-side search across course name, number, professor, and department, combined with department/level/term filters and rating-based sorting. Filter state lives in the URL's search params rather than component state, so any filtered view is shareable and survives a page refresh.
RAG-Powered "Ask the Reviews"
A chat feature (Gemini 2.5 Flash) scoped to a single course's comments: the system prompt injects only that course's student comments as context and explicitly instructs the model to answer from those comments alone, falling back to "I couldn't find that in the reviews" rather than hallucinating. Multi-turn conversation history is preserved across follow-up questions.
Data Ingestion
A seed pipeline parses CTEC source data into structured JSON and pushes it into production via authenticated GraphQL mutations against the Data Connect endpoint, categorizing questions (core rating vs. time-survey vs. demographic) before insertion.
Visualization
Custom rating bars and distribution charts render the 1–6 scale responses and categorical breakdowns as proportional bars, so ratings stay scannable and comparable across courses.

Drift: Listen to Your Body's Boredom
A mobile app concept that detects boredom by fusing digital activity signals and physical biometrics, then surfaces context-aware interventions before the spiral takes hold.

*Figbuild 2026 · 72-hour design challenge · Team of 3 (with Jay Jeon and Elisa Huang)* Boredom is a physical experience, but nobody tracks it. Students sit through lectures, feel their attention slip, and instinctively reach for their phones. The doom-scrolling kicks in. The boredom gets worse. Existing tools like Apple Health or Screen Time show you what happened, but not why. They can't connect physical disengagement to digital behavior or tell you when a boredom spiral is actually starting.
View on Devpost View App
### What We Designed Drift detects boredom by fusing two streams of data: digital activity (tab switching, scroll speed, phone pickup frequency) and physical signals (heart rate variability, eye movement, fidgeting). When the combination hits a threshold, a "boredom spiral detected" alert surfaces a context-aware intervention. It asks what you're doing right now, then suggests a science-backed micro-action tailored to that moment: switching to diagrams mid-lecture, setting a microgoal before the next slide, or chewing gum to restore focus. Beyond real-time intervention, the app gives users a boredom timeline: a dashboard showing when boredom reliably hits, what triggers it, and how long it compounds. The goal isn't just to interrupt the spiral. It's to help users actually understand their attention patterns over time. ### Features
Boredom Detection Engine
Combines digital activity signals (tab switching patterns, scroll speed, phone pickup frequency) and physical biometrics (heart rate variability, eye movement, fidgeting) into a single cumulative attention score. When the score crosses a threshold, Drift knows you're spiraling before you do.
Boredom Spiral Alert
A seamless system overlay that surfaces at exactly the right moment, not as a notification you swipe away, but an in-context interrupt that asks what you're doing right now and offers actions matched to that situation.
Context-Aware Interventions
Drift doesn't give generic advice. It reads your current context (in a lecture, studying, leisure) and suggests science-backed micro-actions accordingly: switching to diagrams, setting a microgoal before the next slide, chewing gum to restore alertness. Actions are tagged by duration so you know what you're committing to.
Boredom Timeline Dashboard
A visual history of your attention patterns over today, 3 days, 7 days, or 90 days. Shows when boredom reliably hits, what triggers it, downstream spiral effects, and your cumulative fragmented attention score, so you can actually learn your patterns and not just react to them.
Granular Permissions and Privacy
Each data type (eye movement tracking, heart rate variability, app switching, scroll patterns, calendar sync) is presented as a separate permission with a plain-language explanation. Raw sensor data never leaves your device via on-device ML, with AES-256 encryption and zero third-party tracking.
Onboarding Flow
A three-step onboarding designed to build trust before asking for anything: a value pitch that reframes boredom as trackable, a transparent permissions flow, and a data sync screen that doubles as the first visual reveal of the Drift aesthetic.
### How We Built It All in Figma. We designed the full end-to-end experience: onboarding (including a deliberate white-to-purple reveal moment as users enter the Drift aesthetic), a granular permissions flow that separates each data type individually for transparency rather than bundling them into one ask, a data syncing screen, the boredom timeline dashboard, and the live intervention overlay. The design system, component library, and all screens were built from scratch in 72 hours. Every UX decision had a rationale. The three-option intervention cards were chunked for memory load, the permissions screen included expandable privacy details because the app handles sensitive biometric data, and the onboarding copy was written to reframe boredom as something trackable rather than something shameful. ### App

From World Learning to World Mirror: LLM-Driven Systems for Cultural Exploration and Self-Reflection
Two LLM-driven systems exploring how place can become a mirror for cultural curiosity and personal reflection.
Developing this project through the Design, Technology and Research program under Delta Lab at Northwestern University, with the close mentorship of Prof. Haoqi Zhang. (I love you DTR ♡)

*Fall 2025.* WorldLearning began with a simple observation: people across cultures seek the same things (fun, connection, belonging, purpose) but realize them in radically different ways. The goal was to make these differences visible, and to encourage curiosity about the social, historical, and cultural factors that shaped them. > People around the world share broad experiential goals such as “relaxing” or “having fun,” but the concrete activities that realize these experiences vary widely by place. Existing tools like search engines, guidebooks, travel blogs, and large language models (LLMs) can answer questions such as “What do people do for fun in Japan?”, yet they typically present one country at a time and require users to already know what to ask. These answer-first interfaces make it hard to see how a single experience is realized differently across countries, or to surface surprising contrasts that might provoke deeper questions. This paper presents WorldLearning, an interactive system that uses an LLM and a world map to help users explore how local people in different countries typically have fun in their free time. Given a user-specified activity (for example, “going to karaoke”), WorldLearning uses an LLM as a scoring model to estimate how typical that activity is as something locals do for fun in each country, and visualizes the resulting scores as a choropleth map with ranking lists and follow-up explanation tools. The system is designed to transform interaction with LLMs from one-shot question–answer exchanges into a dialectical process in which visualized patterns generate new questions that users then probe further. A preliminary study with two participants engaging in guided think-aloud exploration suggests that WorldLearning can surface unexpected global patterns, prompt questions that users would not have asked on their own, and support sustained curiosity-driven inquiry about why everyday experiences are realized differently across countries.
Read the full paper
### Key Features - **Interactive 3D Visualization:** A reactive globe built with Three.js allowing users to spin, zoom, and select countries to visualize data spatially. - **LLM-Driven Scoring:** Uses GPT-4 to dynamically score the "typicality" of activities across different cultures, turning qualitative knowledge into quantitative data. - **Comparative Analysis:** Side-by-side ranking lists and choropleth maps allow users to contrast how different regions prioritize specific experiences. - **Dialectical Exploration:** Designed to prompt follow-up questions rather than just providing static answers, fostering curiosity-driven inquiry. ### Technical Stack - **Frontend:** React (TypeScript), TanStack Start & Router, Tailwind CSS. D3.js and TopoJSON for map visualizations. - **Backend:** Node.js via TanStack Start server functions. Zod for schema validation and custom middleware for auth. - **AI / ML:** OpenAI API (davinci-002 for log-probs, GPT-4 for explanations). Custom tokenization and log-summation logic. - **Tools:** Vite, pnpm, ESLint, Prettier.
As I continued my research, I began asking myself a different question. **Is simply learning facts about differences enough? What were the moments that had actually changed me?** The answer was never a statistic, a map, or a piece of information. One of my best friends is from Cartagena, Colombia. I remember listening to him talk about home, the neighbors who stopped to greet each other, the music, the dancing, the way life seemed to spill out into the streets. There was a warmth, a passion, and a deep love in the way he remembered everything. Weirdly, I felt connected to a place I had never been. But I couldn't reconcile with the contradiction: **How could a country that had experienced so much violence, conflict, and collective trauma still be so full of joy? How could people continue to dance, sing, love, and celebrate after everything they had endured?** At first, I thought I was trying to understand Colombia. Eventually, I realized I was trying to understand myself. When faced with hardships in my own life, my instinct is often to move toward the pain, to make it bigger in my head than it actually is, to analyze it, revisit it, fetishize it. Yet the stories I heard from Colombia seemed to point toward a different form of resilience. Not the denial of suffering, but the refusal to allow suffering to become the entirety of one's life. Joy was not the absence of pain. It was a way of living alongside it. For the first time, I began to wonder whether resilience was not found in endlessly revisiting pain, but in continuing to move despite it.
This realization led me to reconsider the purpose of the project. What stayed with me from encounters with other cultures was not factual knowledge, it was emotional transformation. The most meaningful moments were not when I learned something new about another place. They were when another person's way of living challenged my assumptions about my own.
Fall 2025 → Spring 2026
WorldLearning became WorldMirror.
Rather than treating places as destinations to be learned about, WorldMirror treats places as expressions of human values, priorities, and ways of responding to life's challenges. Each place represents a particular organization of social norms, relationships, histories, and environments. By exploring these systems, users are not only learning about others; they are encountering alternative ways of understanding belonging, community, resilience, and meaning. Places become *models of life organization*, and ultimately mirrors through which users can examine their own assumptions and tensions. > People are often limited to their own perspectives, which are deeply shaped by their surroundings. Place – that is, the geographic location in which people live and interact with one another – is enriched by historical, cultural, and social contexts which subsequently influences how people think and behave. People often perceive locations, especially unfamiliar ones, as inherently distinct from the self, merely as places to visit and learn about rather than as mechanisms for personal development. Yet, people’s internal worlds are shaped by the same forces which shape surroundings. Individual habits, be- liefs, values, and attitudes evolve through exposure to societal, cultural, and environmental pressures. Whether consciously or subconsciously, people make efforts to improve self-concept and overcome personal challenges through reflection, self-awareness, and seeing issues from a new perspective. Oftentimes, it is the last element that enables the first two to occur. There is an opportunity to reconcile people’s internal worlds with their external world, particularly through providing people with contexts that are disparate from their own. In this manner, we welcome alternative perspectives, grounded by physical locations, to help individuals reveal current thought patterns, make com- parisons, and ultimately gain personal insights. In this paper, we present WorldMirror, a system that uses a mixture of LLM discussions and interaction with videos to help users gain a deeper understanding of their problem, learn different ways to approach their problem, and learn about the world. Given a user problem, the LLM prompts the user to learn more about their problem and connect it with different aspects of the user’s life to identify underlying root causes. Then the LLM provides locations around the world that can teach the user new ways of thinking about their problem. Through interacting with a video of people living their daily lives at the location and further discussion with the LLM, the system pushes users to learn more about their problem and the world. A preliminary study with one participant using the system suggests that WorldMirror can understand the user’s problem thoroughly and identify root causes but struggles to help users grow in their own thinking about their problem and the world.
Read the full paper
In the original project, reflection emerged from comparing cultural differences. In WorldMirror, reflection becomes the central mechanism. Users are guided to connect what they observe in an unfamiliar place back to their own experiences. The goal is not simply to understand why a practice exists elsewhere, but to ask what that practice reveals about one's own values, desires, and worldview. I began by believing that learning about the world meant discovering how people are different. Through conversations, travel, and reflection, I came to believe that the most powerful encounters with difference are the ones that reveal our shared humanity. The project shifted from helping users understand other cultures to creating opportunities for the kind of emotional and personal transformation that occurs when another person's story causes us to see ourselves differently.
Time-Resolved Decoding of Working Memory under TRPV1 Activation
Investigating how TRPV1 activation affects neural encoding of working memory using time-resolved decoding on calcium imaging data.

The primary objective is to determine how TRPV1 activation (Capsaicin) affects the neural encoding of working memory. Specifically, does disrupting dopamine signaling (via TRPV1) degrade the brain's ability to maintain task-relevant information during the delay period?
View on GitHub
### Experimental Design - **Subjects:** D1 and D2-receptor expressing mice. - **Task:** A spatial working memory task requiring mice to remember a "Force Direction" (instruction) over a delay period before making a "Choice." - **Conditions:** Baseline (Vehicle 1) · Manipulation (Capsaicin/TRPV1 activation) · Recovery (Vehicle 2)
### Core Methodology: Window-Based Decoding Instead of analyzing the trial as a whole, the project uses a Time-Resolved Decoding approach to pinpoint exactly when information is lost or maintained. 1. **Temporal Slicing:** Trials are split into discrete time windows (e.g., W1–W4) spanning the Delay and Execution phases. 2. **Rigorous Evaluation:** Class balancing (undersampling) ensures a strict 0.5 chance level. Repeated Stratified K-Fold Cross-Validation ensures robustness. ### Key Analyses - **Sensory Maintenance (Delay - Force Dir):** Can the mouse hold the instruction in memory during the delay? - **Motor Planning (Delay - Choice Dir):** Is the mouse planning its movement during the delay? - **Sensory History (Execution - Force Dir):** Is the instruction still represented during the action? - **Motor Execution (Execution - Choice Dir):** How strong is the motor signal during the actual turn? ### Outcome Metrics - **Decoding Accuracy Trajectories:** Plotting accuracy across windows (W1 → W4) to visualize the "memory curve." - **Condition Effects:** Comparing the accuracy curves of Vehicle vs. Capsaicin to quantify the deficit caused by the manipulation. ### Technical Stack - **Core:** Python, NumPy, Pandas - **Data:** h5py (HDF5), scipy.io (MATLAB files) - **ML:** scikit-learn (LogisticRegressionCV, PCA, Stratified K-Fold) - **Viz:** Matplotlib (Accuracy curves, Weight angle heatmaps)
DataBites: A Tangible Museum Exhibit for AI Literacy

DataBites is a tangible museum exhibit that teaches middle schoolers how supervised machine learning works, by having them build one. I designed and built the full interactive interface: from the dataset creation screen to the training animation to the classification results. The UI had to make a CNN pipeline legible to a 10-year-old on a museum floor, with no instructions and no tolerance for confusion.

### Overview **[DataBites](https://www.creativeinterfaces.northwestern.edu/project/453/)** is a physical, hands-on museum installation that teaches kids how machine learning works by letting them train, break, and test a real neural network live in under a minute. Visitors place pizza and sandwich figurines on a board, train a model on the spot, and immediately see how their data choices affect model accuracy on a touchscreen-and-display kiosk built for a museum floor. The exhibit is part of an NSF-funded collaboration between Northwestern University's [Creative Interfaces Research and Design Studio](https://www.creativeinterfaces.northwestern.edu/team/) and Georgia Tech, exploring how embodiment and creativity can foster AI literacy in informal learning environments. DataBites was designed, tested, and evaluated in situ at Chicago's Griffin Museum of Science and Industry. ### Research Focus - Physical manipulation shapes how learners reason about ML in ways a screen-based interface does not automatically preserve. - The study asks whether learners think about the system differently when dataset construction is embodied versus screen-mediated, not just whether they learn the same content. - Data collection includes interaction logs, screen recordings, and learning-talk coding of audio transcripts. - Analysis targets reasoning patterns: whether learners connect prediction errors to dataset decisions, whether they experiment iteratively, and where the interface breaks that chain. - Redesign follows findings: if learners treat the dataset as static, the workspace becomes spatially malleable; if they cannot connect errors to data gaps, model uncertainty becomes visible and repairable. - Core question: can embodied interaction be reimagined for a web interface, not just approximated in one? ### The Experience Each visitor session mirrors a full ML workflow in five fast stages: 1. **Dataset Creation:** A kid arranges food figurines on a board (pizza on the left, sandwiches on the right) and taps **Train**. A camera captures the board as a single screenshot. 2. **Training:** The backend slices the screenshot into six labeled training images and fine-tunes a classifier in about three seconds. In parallel, a slower process visualizes what the model is "looking at." 3. **Testing:** The kid selects nine gallery images as a test set. 4. **Results:** The display shows each test image with the model's prediction so visitors can instantly see where the model succeeded or failed. 5. **Reset:** The session model is discarded and the exhibit resets for the next visitor, with no memory of previous runs. The key pedagogical move is deliberate: the backend does not inspect what object is physically present on each side of the board. It blindly assumes **left = pizza** and **right = sandwich**. If a visitor intentionally places a sandwich on the pizza side, the model learns the wrong label and fails later. It teaches garbage in, garbage out through direct interaction. ### Design Principles - No instructions and no facilitator: the interface had to explain itself to a 10-year-old in under 30 seconds. - Each stage of the ML pipeline (dataset creation, training, classification, results) is a distinct visible moment, not a background process. - Animation playback speed recalculates at runtime to match narration clip duration, keeping voice and motion locked together as audio changes. - The dataset creation screen is designed to feel like a continuation of the physical table interaction, not a mode switch. - Model failures are the point: the results screen makes misclassifications specific enough to trace back to dataset decisions. - Button feedback uses image swaps and CSS scale transforms instead of hover states, built for deliberate single taps on a kiosk. ### Technical Architecture DataBites is a full-stack, dual-screen system: - **Backend (Python/Flask):** One Flask app exposes training, testing, and generated-asset endpoints (`/api/train`, `/api/test`, `/api/masks`) plus static routes for debug slices and segmentation masks. - **Two-stage model design:** A ResNet18 backbone is pre-trained offline in [Databites-MoE](https://github.com/Creative-Interfaces/Databites-MoE), loaded frozen at server start, and converted to a feature encoder by replacing its final layer with identity. Each session then trains a fresh `nn.Linear(512, 2)` head (~1,026 parameters) on top of frozen features. This enables genuine live training on CPU in about three seconds over 25 epochs on six images. - **Background SAM segmentation:** Meta's Segment Anything Model runs in a background thread, detects visual regions, and groups them into "large" and "small" features by pixel area. Since SAM takes roughly two minutes on CPU, `/api/train` returns immediately after fast head training, and the frontend polls `/api/masks` every 10 seconds until segmentation is ready. - **Frontend (React):** A touch controller and a large display run as separate windows of the same React app and synchronize in real time via the native **BroadcastChannel API**, avoiding websockets for UI state sharing. ### Engineering Challenges Solved - **Making real training feel instant:** Decoupled a fast disposable linear head from a slow frozen backbone so training could run live on museum PCs without GPUs. - **Keeping UX responsive despite slow vision inference:** Ran SAM asynchronously and polled for completion instead of blocking the interaction loop. - **Fixing cross-window sync bugs:** Resolved duplicate BroadcastChannel sends and corrected schema mismatches (`item.prediction` vs `item.predicted`) that caused incorrect display labels. - **Tuning segmentation for real museum conditions:** Iterated SAM area thresholds to better separate large objects (food items) from smaller toppings under noisy lighting and camera variability. - **Improving model performance on physical artifacts:** Expanded and retrained the backbone dataset from 200 to 252 images focused on the exhibit objects, improving held-out accuracy from 87.5% to 97.3%. - **Hardening deployment on shared hardware:** Diagnosed environment-specific issues (including Node version mismatch failures) and established a git workflow that avoids conflicts from runtime-generated files. ### Tech Stack `Python` · `Flask` · `PyTorch` (ResNet18 + linear probe) · `Segment Anything Model (SAM)` · `React` · `BroadcastChannel API` · `Flask-CORS` ### Why It Is Interesting DataBites compresses the machine learning lifecycle into a 60-second physical experience: collect data, train a model, evaluate results, and observe failure modes. The core challenge was not maximizing benchmark accuracy. It was making a real model fast enough, transparent enough, and robust enough to run repeatedly in front of museum visitors on commodity CPU hardware.
